# Elasticsearch 7 collapse public contract

This page exposes the collapse call contract and wire protocol separately; callers Fang Ke can directly use the public entry points below.

- `new \Elastica\Collapse()` creates a collapse object.
- `setFieldname($fieldName): self` sets `field`.
- `setInnerHits(\Elastica\Collapse\InnerHits): self` sets named inner hits; this type inherits from `\Elastica\Query\InnerHits` and supports `setName(string): self`.
- `setMaxConcurrentGroupSearches(int): self` sets the number of concurrent group searches.
- `\Elastica\Query::setCollapse(\Elastica\Collapse): self` accepts this object and serializes the collapse request.
- `\Elastica\QueryBuilder::collapse()->inner_hits(): \Elastica\Collapse\InnerHits` returns an object that can be configured further.

Behavioral acceptance also checks public calls, field, named inner hits, integer concurrency, and Query serialization; it must not be approved based only on source-code strings or a single fixed gold path.

Field-name setter accepts string names without a newly imposed scalar type declaration. All setters are fluent. Reusing field, inner hits, or concurrency setters replaces the old value. Inner hits also support setSize(int): self. A string concurrency value raises native TypeError for strict_types=1 callers.

## Pagination and suggest contracts

Query::setFrom(int): self and Query::setSize(int $size = 10): self accept and retain integer pagination values, including zero, and serialize them as from and size. Repeated calls replace the previous value. String, float, boolean, and null arguments raise native TypeError in strict_types=1 callers without changing existing pagination state.

QueryBuilder\DSL\Suggest::term(string $name, string $field): Elastica\Suggest\Term, phrase(string $name, string $field): Elastica\Suggest\Phrase, and completion(string $name, string $field): Elastica\Suggest\Completion must preserve each caller's name and field and return the corresponding configurable suggestion object. Both arguments of all three factories reject non-string scalar values and null with native TypeError in strict_types=1 callers.

# DSN Configuration and Aggregation Lookup Migration

This page originally tied two things to transport: migrating typed DSN configuration from the debug entry point to users' normal calls, and folding strict aggregation lookup names into the same round of checks. That assessment remains in the previous version because it was used to set the order of follow-up checks at the time; it should no longer be treated as a statement of module ownership.

The old record used this workflow:

```text
Debug entry point
  ↓ Retain the return value or raw diagnostics
Guzzle transport
  ↓ Tentative go-ahead if no transport exception is observed
Normal calls
```

The "go-ahead" here later turned out to be just a premature working judgment. `lib/Elastica/Transport/Guzzle.php` provides only transport-adjacent context. The file header shows `Elastica\Connection`, along with references to three exception types: `GuzzleException`, `PartialShardFailureException`, and `ResponseException`. This is not enough to attribute DSN type handling or the aggregation-name lookup rules to this file. The old steps treated the exception branch as a common exit point for compatibility checks, which could make it look as though both checks had gone through the same implementation path.

### Migration Approach Retained in the First Draft

The first draft required capturing the return value or raw diagnostics through the debug entry point first, then running the same DSN through normal calls. The purpose was not to compare every behavior of the two entry points, but to avoid inspecting the configuration only in the debug environment. If normal calls cannot retain the return value or raw diagnostics, return to the old entry point to capture the state; do not yet treat "no transport exception was seen" as evidence that the configuration migration is complete.

At the time, no DSN field table or list of aggregation API names was written up. Do not fill in those details from this page; what it preserves is the old migration sequence, not field definitions.

### Follow-up Review Notes

ESC-209 narrowed the scope of the check: run `typed DSN configuration` through users' normal calls, not just the debug entry point, and retain the return value or raw diagnostics. The old entry point still has a use in this migration: if differences appear in normal calls, first restore the old path that can capture diagnostics, then run the same configuration through the normal entry point again. This restores the observation method; it does not establish the transport file as the place where configuration is implemented.

```text
Old: debug entry point → transport observation → normal calls
New: normal calls → retain the return value or raw diagnostics
                  └─return to the debug entry point to capture the state if differences appear
```

This note did not confirm any specific DSN types, defaults, or normalization rules. The old page's statement, "proceed if there is no transport exception," only explains the decision not to stop at the time; it is not a finding from the current checks.

ESC-226 point to another unfinished migration track: for `strict aggregation lookup names`, the relevant module maintainer should check the behavior in the current version and provide an entry point for further checks. The first draft appended this to the DSN checks only because both items were part of the same compatibility wrap-up, not because they shared configuration handling. If aggregation-name results differ now, first retain the name, call site, and raw diagnostics returned; do not start by changing DSN just to reuse the old steps, and do not use transport exceptions as a substitute for checking aggregation lookups.

This page therefore retains two sets of guidance that are not entirely consistent: the old workflow still says to start from `Guzzle.php`, while the later notes require evidence to be captured separately from normal calls and the relevant module entry point. The former helps reconstruct the investigation steps taken at the time, while the latter only separates what had been incorrectly combined; it does not provide the final name set for strict aggregation lookup names.

### Steps That Can Still Be Followed

1. When handling DSN, first run the configuration through normal calls and save the return value or raw diagnostics.
2. If that entry point cannot capture the state, restore the old debug-entry-point path solely to obtain comparable diagnostics; then return to normal calls.
3. When aggregation names differ, take the name and call site to the relevant module's entry point for further checks; do not reuse the go-ahead judgment from DSN.
4. If you need to look at both topics together, you can refer to the DOC-20 record on nullable client callbacks / collapse builder facade; it is not evidence of how these two objects are implemented.

The old page did not finish verifying the aggregation names, nor did it update this page with the current module entry point. This gap is left open to avoid recombining the two check paths that were later separated into a single transport migration step.

# Scroll Cleanup and Distance Request Decision

This revision retains a starting point that has since been revised: empty-page scroll cleanup and distance-feature request integration were originally scheduled for the same review round, not because they had been confirmed to share an implementation, but because the old investigation records both led to `lib/Elastica/Search.php`. As the freeze approached closure, this combined arrangement had a practical benefit: start with an object that exposes requests, results, and clues about result construction together, without expanding the search scope before runtime evidence was available.

The initial draft mistakenly described a "shared reading entry point" as something close to "shared completion criteria." These two things now need to be separated. Search can remain the starting point for looking back through the code; empty-page cleanup and distance feature integration each require evidence that establishes their own status. Later counterexamples exposed precisely this distinction, so this page no longer treats positive observations on one side as proof of completion on the other.

## Early Assessment Retained

The assumption from the previous version has not been deleted: if the area around the Search object can explain the continuous relationship from request to result, both issues can be examined together in a single compatibility review. This assumption explains the investigation sequence at the time and prevents later readers from mistakenly thinking that the two efforts were completely independent tasks from the outset.

But that statement rested on an overly broad premise. The empty-page issue is not about "whether a result object exists near Search," but about what successful and failed scroll calls each leave behind after visible results have already been obtained. The distance feature issue is also not about "whether a configuration or sample can be found," but about whether the request actually takes effect when the real entry point and the sample results are inconsistent. Being able to start reading along the same path for both issues does not make the two kinds of observations the same.

Therefore, the statement "looking at Search first lets us close both out together" is retired as of this revision. It is retained only as an early working assessment and will no longer be used to determine freeze status.

## This Decision

The decision is to split the review into two record tracks that share Search as an entry point for verification, but do not share completion criteria.

- empty-page scroll cleanup must retain the visible results of successful and failed calls separately. With counterexamples already on record, results from either side alone cannot establish that cleanup has been confirmed.
- distance-feature request integration must be checked in a real CI run to determine whether it takes effect. Neither the existence of configuration files nor the existence of sample text can substitute for that run result.
- The two record tracks may reference the same entry file, but each updates only its own status. Observations about empty pages cannot serve as confirmation for distance-feature, and vice versa.
- This decision does not assign implementation ownership. It only specifies what evidence can count as a review conclusion during the freeze, preventing static inspection, the existence of samples, and actual execution from being treated as the same kind of signal.

This split does not expand the issues into a new architectural overhaul. It simply retracts the overly strong inference in the initial draft: a shared entry point is a convenience for organizing the investigation, not evidence that the behavior is already the same.

## The Empty-Page Track

ESC-211 preserves the inventory of observed empty-page scroll behavior. It requires the visible results from one successful call and one failed call to be retained separately; counterexamples were added later, and one aspect of cleanup remains unconfirmed. The conclusion that can be drawn here is narrow: the results of a successful call cannot stand in for those of a failed call, nor can the absence of the expected behavior in a failed call be used to infer that cleanup on the success path is complete.

"Unconfirmed" should not be rewritten as a specific exception, a particular piece of cleanup code, or a particular lifecycle stage. The existing records do not provide those details. It means this track still lacks observations sufficient to establish conclusively the cleanup status after an empty page, not that every result-related dependency in the Search file needs to be explained again.

The responsibility of the empty-page record is limited to preserving results from both types of calls. If new results are added later, first determine whether they belong to a successful or failed call, then add them to the corresponding side. Collapsing both sides into a brief "empty page has been handled" status is exactly what this decision is intended to avoid.

## The Distance Feature Track

ESC-228 records a mismatch between the real entry point for distance-feature and the sample results. The check it leaves is explicit: confirm in a real CI run whether distance-feature request integration takes effect, rather than treating the existence of a configuration file as a run result.

The difference between this requirement and the empty-page track is not which issue matters more, but what evidence is acceptable for confirmation. The empty-page track needs to preserve visible results from both types of calls; the distance feature track needs confirmation from an actual run. Even if both start by looking back through Search, a static object, a sample, or call results from the other issue should not be prematurely recorded as proof that distance requests have been integrated.

Until runtime confirmation is obtained for the distance feature, this page records it only as an integration target awaiting validation. The mismatch between the real entry point and the sample is itself enough to reject the claim that "the sample looks reasonable, so the request has taken effect"; it is not enough to infer where in construction, serialization, or transport the mismatch occurs.

## Approaches Compared at the Time

|Approach|Convenience retained|Reason for rejection or adoption|
|---|---|---|
|Treat both issues as a single Search compatibility change|A centralized review entry point and shorter records|Not adopted. The results from both types of calls for the empty-page issue and the CI results for the distance feature are not interchangeable evidence.|
|Use configuration or samples as proof that the distance feature is integrated|No need to wait for runtime confirmation|Not adopted. When the real entry point and sample results are inconsistent, the existence of configuration cannot answer whether the request takes effect.|
|Record only the empty-page issue first, then move the distance feature out of the freeze|A narrower immediate scope|Not adopted. distance-feature request integration is already part of this review round and cannot disappear from the records merely because run results are not yet available.|
|Store results separately while sharing the Search entry point|Follow the existing reading clues while preserving separate assessment criteria|Adopted.|

The fourth option in the table is the only approach formally adopted on this page. It does not mean that the two issues necessarily share an implementation, nor does it require tracing every possible call edge without additional evidence. The actual review only needs updates according to the respective evidence types: add results from both types of calls for the empty-page issue, and results from a real CI run for the distance feature.

## Scope of the Search Entry Point

`lib/Elastica/Search.php` remains a suitable starting point for looking up this history. The `Elastica\Exception\InvalidException`, `Elastica\ResultSet\BuilderInterface`, and `Elastica\ResultSet\DefaultBuilder` at the top of the file indicate its proximity to result construction and also explain why the early investigation started here.

However, imports do not automatically show how the scroll context is handled afterward, nor do they show the actual request results for distance-feature. Their role on this page is to define the reading starting point: first look for clues in the relationship between requests and results in Search, then return to the respective review records. Elevating this static adjacency directly into a runtime conclusion would repeat the initial draft's mistaken merging.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> MergedReview
    MergedReview --> SeparateConfirmation: Counterexample added
    SeparateConfirmation --> EmptyPageObservation
```

- Keep the parameter, but stop passing it into the downstream connection configuration;
- Keep the existing interface first, locate the places in `_initConnections`, `_prepareConnectionParams`, and `setConfig` that actually use the logging object, then decide where to remove it.

If only one entry point can be verified, that is not grounds to remove the other.

# Legacy Logger Retirement Plan

This trial covers the legacy logger entry points still exposed on Client. The goal is not to redesign all logging behavior, but to establish which layer can actually be removed as compatibility support is wound down: the public constructor parameter, its propagation within Client, or the old conventions in the connection configuration. These are not the same change. Bundling them into a single deletion would make it impossible to distinguish caller errors from connection-layer errors.

The initial draft treated `LoggerInterface $logger = null` as a sign that "behavior should be equivalent without a logger." On review, that can only remain a working hypothesis. A nullable parameter means a call can omit it; it does not mean that omission produces the same result as explicitly passing an object. In addition to the constructor of `Client`, the file has `_initConnections`, `_prepareConnectionParams` and `setConfig` nearby; these locations need to be examined individually in terms of data flow. The signature alone cannot determine the scope of retirement.

The constructor entry point currently identifiable from `lib/Elastica/Client.php` is:

```php
public function __construct(array $config = [], $callback = null, LoggerInterface $logger = null)
```

The file also imports `Action`, `ConnectionException`, `InvalidException` and `AbstractScript` at the top. These imports show that Client sits alongside several objects, but are not evidence that any specific branch consumes the logger. This review should focus on post-construction connection preparation, without pulling bulk operations, scripts or exception handling into the trial's scope.

## Trade-offs in the Earlier Plan

**Option A: Remove the third constructor parameter directly.**

This gives the cleanest API surface and is the easiest way to expose downstream call sites immediately on upgrade. However, it collapses two questions into one: whether legacy calls still exist, and whether Client merely passes the logger to the connection layer. The former would show up as a failed call; the latter might only become apparent after a connection is established. For the Horizon 7 cleanup, this mix of failures is not a suitable way to establish scope.

**Option B: Keep the signature but stop handling the parameter internally.**

This can temporarily avoid breaking constructor calls outright, but if the parameter still affects behavior through connection initialization, the interface would fail silently. Callers would see that the parameter can still be passed, but it would have no effect; that is harder to discover than an explicit compatibility change. Unless we can clearly document that the object never reaches downstream arguments, we will not adopt this silent approach.

**Option C: Map the shortest propagation chain first, then choose the removal point.**

This option keeps the existing signature as the boundary of the trial. Start the check at `__construct` and follow only as far as `_initConnections` and `_prepareConnectionParams`; if `setConfig` changes the same configuration, also record whether that happens before the connection is established. The trial does not need to establish everything Client is responsible for; it only needs to answer where the logger goes along this part of the chain.

This round adopts Option C. It is not a long-term commitment to retaining the legacy logger. It avoids treating removal as a done deal before the relationship between the entry point and propagation is understood.

## Recording the Trial

Keep two minimal input cases for each check: construction without the third parameter, and construction with an explicitly supplied logger. For each case, record only three things: whether the object is stored during construction, whether it is read while preparing connection parameters, and whether it is passed on to another object during connection initialization. If a stage has no visible references, record "not confirmed at this stage"; do not record the absence of a reference as a confirmed removal.

`setConfig` needs its own entry. Configuration set after construction may not follow the same path as constructor arguments; even if the two have similar names, do not merge them based on names alone. Only include it in this retirement trial if it is confirmed to overwrite the same logging-related value. Otherwise, it is simply another configuration entry point in Client.

Do not modify `getVersion` during the trial, or use a version query as a substitute example of logger behavior. It is in the same class as the constructor, but does not show the logger's propagation path. Likewise, connection exceptions can suggest when to investigate, but are not a reason to remove the parameter.

## Acceptable Outcomes and Withdrawal

If neither constructor input case has any logger usage points before connection preparation, and `setConfig` does not reintroduce the object, a separate change can be opened to remove the interface; this plan only records the locations needed to support that conclusion. If the parameter is stored or passed on, do not remove the signature during the freeze. First complete the record of actual consumers and caller scope, then decide.

If explicitly passing a logger and omitting the parameter lead to different branches in connection preparation, do not use a transition that keeps the signature but ignores the parameter either. That would hide an existing difference in the compatibility layer. In that case, withdraw the retirement trial, keep the existing entry point, and handle the difference as a subsequent compatibility issue.

ESC-212 can serve as a starting point for hands-on investigation. The card notes that the actual legacy logger entry point does not match the sample results; the review record should add the location of the corresponding rule file and the final list of findings, rather than using sample names in place of actual call sites.

The unresolved question is whether, if the logger is used only by the connection layer, the retirement change should target Client's public interface or the connection layer's configuration contract. Until the full propagation chain is visible, do not prescribe the same removal plan for both locations.

# Total Hits Tracking Troubleshooting Tree

This page remains under the old entry point because, when field regression testing mentioned track-total-hits fidelity, the earliest available lead was on the query DSL side. It is not a release process that has already been tightened up; the stopping points below did not automatically cease to apply just because cards were added later.

The initial draft listed `lib/Elastica/QueryBuilder/DSL/Query.php` as the first location to open. That wording was somewhat misleading: jumping to this file based on the issue name and call name does not mean this is where total hits information is determined. This entry point is still useful, especially when you need to confirm which types are near request construction; it just cannot replace cross-checking the request, response, and caller.

The adjacent relationships visible at the top of the file at the time were as follows:

```php
use Elastica\Exception\NotImplementedException;
use Elastica\Query\AbstractQuery;
use Elastica\Query\AbstractSpanQuery;
use Elastica\Query as BaseQuery;
```

These references can show that the file is near query objects, but cannot show whether a particular regression was triggered by exception handling, a regular query, or a span query. The old notes used these four names as a basis for narrowing the scope; retain that step, but withdraw the implication that it can locate the execution point.

## First, Break Down the Case

When feedback says "total hits look wrong," first collect the artifacts from both ends of the same call. Here, "the same call" means that the request sent by the caller can be matched to the response it reads, not two screenshots that look similar. Without this pair of artifacts, every subsequent branch will only make the speculation more elaborate.

```text
Regression testing reports a mismatch in track-total-hits fidelity
|
+-- Is the request body still available?
|   |
|   +-- No
|   |   `-- Stop trying to locate the issue. Record the missing request-side artifacts; do not infer DSL from the result numbers.
|   |
|   `-- Yes
|       |
|       +-- Is the response envelope returned by the same call available?
|       |   |
|       |   +-- No
|       |   |   `-- Save the request-side artifacts and wait for the response-side artifacts to be added. At this point, you cannot determine whether the read is incorrect.
|       |   |
|       |   `-- Yes
|       |       |
|       |       +-- Are the requests on both sides exactly the same?
|       |       |   |
|       |       |   +-- No
|       |       |   |   `-- First trace back through the caller and request construction; do not attribute the difference to how the results are read.
|       |       |   |
|       |       |   `-- Yes
|       |       |       |
|       |       |       +-- Does the total hits information in the response retain the same shape?
|       |       |       |   |
|       |       |       |   +-- No
|       |       |       |   |   `-- Record the original shape and relation information, and check where the response envelope enters the client.
|       |       |       |   |
|       |       |       |   `-- Yes
|       |       |       |       |
|       |       |       |       +-- Does the caller read it the same way?
|       |       |       |           |
|       |       |       |           +-- No
|       |       |       |           |   `-- The issue remains at the caller's interpretation boundary; include the values before and after reading.
|       |       |       |           |
|       |       |       |           `-- Yes
|       |       |       |               `-- Then check the code around query construction and transport; only now return to Query.php.
```

"A different shape" should not be reduced to a larger or smaller number. The response envelope for Horizon 7 may provide a structured total hits value and its relation; if the original value has not been saved, the number displayed on the page is not enough to identify which layer the fidelity issue lies in. The old notes collectively referred to such cases as "total count truncation," but that judgment should no longer be the starting point for troubleshooting, and the original wording has been left in place solely to explain why people used to look for the query builder first.

## How to Use the Query.php Branch

Only enter this path after the request body has been retained, the response envelope has been matched to it, and the caller's reading method has not already revealed a difference. First confirm that the query-object neighborhood you are examining is one in which the current issue can be reproduced, rather than starting modifications merely because the filenames are similar. The scope of what you can do here is narrow: check whether the object involved in the issue falls in the vicinity of `AbstractQuery`, `AbstractSpanQuery`, or the base `Query`; if it does not, immediately return to the caller or the response-reading code.

If the file contains only the type references above and no object relationships that connect to the request from the case, stop here. Continuing to search laterally within the DSL directory usually produces more similar names, but does not supply the actual request. The initial draft did not spell out this stopping point, leading people to mistake "looked at Query.php" for having verified the query side; now, recording the findings in the following format is enough:

| Available artifacts | What can be determined | What still cannot be determined |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Only the file entry point and type references | This entry point is close to query DSL | Who constructed this request and where the value is read |
| Request body and response envelope retained as a pair | The request and response shapes can be compared | Whether the caller interprets relation as expected |
| Same request, same shape, consistent reading method | The code around construction can be investigated further | Whether this file actually contains the specific implementation |

The last column in the table is not a to-do list. It is a stop-work condition: without new artifacts, do not turn a directory browse into a conclusion.

## Previous Recovery Actions

The old version recommended "roll back the query side first, then check the total count." That statement is now only a historical record. It treated rollback as an inspection method, conflating restoring the incident environment with identifying the cause: if the request body or response envelope was not saved, even if the results differ before and after the rollback, you cannot know whether the comparison still involves the same request.

Therefore, anyone still using the old entry point should first retain the pre-rollback request, response, and values read by the caller. If the rollback entry point itself is unclear, do not temporarily designate a query class as a substitute entry point. The card calls for filling in the workflow that actually ran and the rollback entry point from the build logs; until these two artifacts are available, this page provides no specific rollback actions.

Another old habit was to classify the case as "unsupported" on seeing `NotImplementedException`. This has also been abandoned. The presence of this exception type at the top of the file does not show that a particular request triggered it. Only record it as the branch for this case when the failure output or call path clearly points to that exception; otherwise, leave it "not linked."

## Minimum Record for Handoff

You do not need to copy the entire log for every rerun, but retain at least the following items so that later comparisons do not mix up two requests:

- The request body provided by the caller, and the call site it came from;
- The corresponding complete response envelope, especially the original structure of the total hits value and its relation;
- The value or assessment after the caller reads it, not just the final number displayed;
- Whether you went into `Query.php`, and the object relationships actually found there;
- If a recovery attempt was made, whether the request was still the same before and after the attempt.

If any of these items is missing, record the missing item and stop at the previous level; do not add "should be the same" in the notes. The purpose of this record is not to squeeze all feedback into the same type of failure, but to avoid conflating request construction, the response envelope, and caller interpretation as a single issue.

ESC-213 still list the actual execution steps, the responsible workflow, and the rollback entry point as pending additions. When more artifacts are added later, place them under the appropriate branches first: build logs can establish the execution entry point, raw requests and responses can establish the actual case, and caller results can establish the interpretation boundary. They are not substitutes for one another.

What is confirmed for the stored track_total_hits value, without closing the unconfirmed branches above, is that true stays true, false stays false rather than 1 or 0, and an integer such as 250 stays that integer. The most recent review confirmed only that someone had taken on the work and started addressing it; no new rerun results were available that could close the unconfirmed branches. Therefore, retain the old reminder to "rerun through the same entry point," but do not describe it as completed verification.

# History of Aggregation Metadata

This page began with a very narrow lead. When searching for aggregation metadata lifecycle, the earlier investigation repeatedly led to `lib/Elastica/QueryBuilder/DSL/Aggregation.php`. At the time, there was no complete call record to cross-check, so the filename and the declarations of several aggregation classes became the focus of the discussion. Subsequent notes did not replace this lead, but gradually reframed it from an "answer" to an "entry point".

That is also why this page has been retained. It is not the current documentation for aggregation metadata, but material left from a scoping decision during the freeze: what could be seen directly from the path, what was merely inferred from names at the time, and why the original inference was not extended further.

## The Earlier Approach of Finding the File by Name First

The initial approach was straightforward. The issue name contained aggregation, and the call name also pointed to DSL, so `Aggregation.php` was opened, and the class names at the top of the file were used to infer potentially adjacent objects. This was a fast way to locate things: readers could get a local view of aggregation DSL without first knowing the complete request path.

The direct dependencies recorded at the time were:

```text
use Elastica\Aggregation\Avg;
use Elastica\Aggregation\AvgBucket;
use Elastica\Aggregation\BucketScript;
use Elastica\Aggregation\Cardinality;
```

The first draft presented these declarations alongside the file location, assuming they were already enough to establish the main location of the metadata lifecycle. That wording was too hasty. `Avg`, `AvgBucket`, `BucketScript`, and `Cardinality` only show that these aggregation classes are visible at the top of the file, not where metadata first appears, which objects it passes through, or who reads it.

The earlier framing was not deleted. On the one hand, it accurately explains why the investigation started with this PHP file; on the other, searching via aggregation DSL is still more effective than starting from scratch. What needed correcting was the interpretation of "pointing here": it records a search action, not a confirmed implementation boundary.

## The Trade-off Actually Chosen at the Time

Two approaches were compared during the review.

The first was to treat `lib/Elastica/QueryBuilder/DSL/Aggregation.php` directly as the home of the aggregation metadata lifecycle. This wording would quickly bring the file, class names, and topic together, and would read smoothly. But it would mistake local declarations for runtime evidence; if metadata propagation or consumption were later found to happen elsewhere, the page would conflate the entry point with the scope of responsibility.

The second was to keep the file as the starting point for follow-up tracing. The file path, module type, and direct dependencies could all remain; actions within the lifecycle would only be assigned once actual calls became available. This approach did not immediately provide a complete explanation, but it preserved the object boundaries that could be confirmed at the time.

The record adopts the second approach. The decision does not deny the relationship between DSL and the aggregation classes, but stops using paths and names as substitutes for facts about calls. The earlier page's reading of "this is the main landing point" was later narrowed to "this is the first hop".

| Object seen at the time | Treatment in the record |
| --- | --- |
| `Aggregation.php` | Retained as an entry point for follow-up tracing |
| Aggregation classes at the top of the file | Recorded as local declarations |
| Metadata generation and propagation | Not inferred from the filename |
| Most recent actual call | Still to be added |
| Result seen by the user | Still to be added |

This table only sets out the decisions made at the time, not a lifecycle model added later. In particular, "there are aggregation class declarations" must not be read as "we already know how aggregation results are returned to the caller".

## Notes Added After Image Cleanup

The follow-up investigation did not proceed as originally planned. ESC-216 was marked Blocked for a time, with the recorded reason being that the required old-version image had already been cleaned up; the item later returned to To Do. This change brought no new conclusions about the code, but it changed what the page needed to preserve.

When the image is unavailable, the easiest thing to do is to follow the old path and fill in a seemingly coherent account of the calls. That would make the page read more completely, but would hide the missing version-specific material. The alternative is to retain the path, visible declarations, and unconfirmed items separately. The latter was chosen here, so cleanup of the old image was recorded only as the reason the review was blocked, not as any lifecycle conclusion.

The same round of documentation also left a correction: in the Aggregation DSL section, one aspect of the aggregation metadata lifecycle is still unconfirmed. It did not specify which class, part of a request, or type of result that aspect corresponded to; this page does not expand that statement into a complete design judgment either. Its only purpose is to undo the prematurely conclusive tone of the first draft.

Below is the simple state diagram used at the time to depict the search status. It describes how the path was used, not an object state machine in the code:

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> FileEntry
    FileEntry --> LocalDeclarations
    LocalDeclarations --> PendingVerification
    PendingVerification --> FileEntry: Continue tracing back
```

"PendingVerification" in the diagram includes the most recent actual call, how it was made, and the result seen by the user. It does not additionally specify which object to look at for answers, because the available material does not establish that relationship.

## The Earlier Approach That Was Retained

Guiding readers to this file by the issue name and call name is the earlier approach that was retained. It is not ineffective: for anyone who needs to locate aggregation DSL quickly, the path and four direct dependencies are still concrete, usable starting points. The problem with the earlier approach was that it had been written as though it could determine the lifecycle on its own.

This was explicitly corrected later. The file location provides local adjacency, not the complete runtime sequence; class names provide a direction for reading, not proof of where metadata comes from. Once the two were separated, the old record remained useful as a reference, but had much less potential to mislead.

This kind of trade-off also has practical costs. Promoting a path to the implementation home can reduce the time spent continuing to check references in the short term, but it leads later readers to look for problems within the wrong boundary. Keeping it only as an entry point requires continued checking of actual calls, and leaves gaps on the page. During the freeze, the latter cost was accepted because the material available at the time was not sufficient to support the former wording.

## How to Read the Page After This Correction

Looking back at v1 now, "main landing point" can only be understood in its historical context. It describes the initial search result, not the implementation location of the metadata lifecycle. The image-related blocker added in v2 also only explains why the review was not completed, and cannot be used in reverse to prove that a particular calling method must have existed in the old version.

ESC-216 is used here to navigate to the item awaiting investigation. The local description left on the card is to find the most recent actual call that reported aggregation metadata lifecycle, and add how it was made and the result seen by the user. This corresponds to the decision on this page: the card preserves the direction of the investigation, while the page preserves why the DSL file was not designated as the implementation home for the entire lifecycle at the time.

The adjacent DOC-27 discusses strict pagination offsets, and should not be used to fill the gaps in aggregation metadata. The two pages can be referenced alongside each other, but their topics, objects, and judgments at the time are independent. This boundary was not made clear in the early draft and was only added later.

Reading can still begin at this path: first examine the local declarations and direct references in the current revision, then look for the most recent actual call. If a call is found later, the actual objects and actions should be added, rather than rewriting the guesses in the old paragraphs to sound more certain. At a minimum, distinguish where the call enters, at which step metadata appears, which party reads it, and in what form the result is seen.

## The Decision Retained

The final decision retained on this page is: `lib/Elastica/QueryBuilder/DSL/Aggregation.php` can serve as an entry point for tracing the aggregation metadata lifecycle, but it cannot be designated as the implementation home of the complete lifecycle solely on the basis of the issue name, call name, path, or dependencies at the top of the file.

This decision is more conservative than the first draft, and closer to the material left at the time. The earlier direction of investigation remains, the declarations of the four aggregation classes remain usable, and the blocker caused by image cleanup has not been erased. Objects that have not yet been confirmed remain unconfirmed until the actual call, how it was made, and the user-visible result can be added back.

# Decision on cached quality signals and original run evidence

The trade-off between cached data and original run evidence did not lead to an interface change. The Quality Signal Dashboard needs to preserve the run associated with the current revision, rather than treat records compiled afterward as the original run itself. The existing page is still handled by `docs/adj-elastica/decisions/elastica-quality-signal-cache-vs-original-state-tradeoffs.md`; cached material and original run material can coexist on it, but serve different purposes.

## Retained early assessment

The initial draft framed the issue in terms of `serialized request body` and `public PHP API`. At the time, the two pieces of material showed different failure exits, so the preference was to split API out to avoid documenting different exits as the same path. There was not enough evidence from callers to support this assessment; in particular, who actually used `request transport` was still unclear.

> The original draft's provisional position: continue along `serialized request body`, or split `public PHP API` out on its own; if the two pieces are later confirmed to lead to the same exit, reverse the split.

That original position is retained here because it explains why caching was once considered an isolation mechanism. It is no longer the decision in effect. Subsequent review did not establish that splitting API out could restore the original run context, nor that it could resolve the stop at the exit entry point.

## Boundaries identified after the second pass

During that pass, `Elasticsearch 7 response envelope` was retained for comparison. It can help identify differences between the materials, but is not a reason to extend the Quality Signal Dashboard's scope to shared interfaces. Matching names, similar output, or a single green cleanup pass are not enough to bring behavior from elsewhere into this decision.

ESCA-008 spelled out more concretely what should be retained before handback: the exit code, quality signals, and the final log segment. If any of the three is missing, later readers can only see the compiled results and cannot tell where the original run ended. Preserving the current revision therefore no longer means simply keeping a version label; it means keeping this set of run evidence from just before release.

ESCA-012 made the exit action a separate issue. The records included cases where, after switching accounts or workspaces, progress stopped at the exit entry point. This observation does not imply that all entry points behave the same way, and a local rollback must not be described as a full recovery. The temporary task was later canceled because it no longer had any consumers. The cancellation ended that temporary arrangement; it did not confirm the state of the entry point.

## Decision in effect

This page now adopts the following approach.

1. The environment will not be rebuilt for the current revision to fill gaps in the cache. A rebuild would produce another run; it can serve as a new comparison, but cannot replace the run evidence already retained before release.
2. Original run evidence is the primary record for assessment. The exit code, quality signals, and final log segment saved before handback must be retained with the current revision.
3. Cached records may continue to serve as an entry point for organizing and finding material, but are not a substitute for original run evidence. Even when a green result appears in the cache, it must still be possible to trace it back to the corresponding original record.
4. `public PHP API` will not be changed as part of this decision. The earlier proposal to split API out is listed among the options not adopted, keeping unconfirmed caller scope out of this decision.
5. Verify the exit action separately. It is related to retaining quality signals, but has a different completion criterion.

This decision applies only to material already retained by the Quality Signal Dashboard. It does not specify what other projects should retain or draw cross-project compatibility conclusions from the comparison material.

## Options not adopted

**Keep only the cache.** This would make it easier to find things on the page, but would lose the original relative positions of the exit code, quality signals, and final log segment. If the cache contents were later reorganized, readers would not be able to tell from them whether a green result came from the same run.

**Rebuild the environment, then fill in the records.** This option was considered because material from a rebuilt environment might be more complete; but it cannot answer where the current revision exited at the time. This decision preserves the original run evidence. If a rebuild happens, it can only serve as a later comparison and must not overwrite the old records.

**Split API out as originally proposed.** Different failure exits were the starting point, not sufficient reason for a split. Without information on how `request transport` was actually used, changing `public PHP API` would expand what was a localized retention issue into an interface change, so this option is not adopted.

## Checkpoints for follow-up review

ESCA-017 require actual consumers to start from the current revision and record the first break in the navigation chain; ESCA-021 likewise require following the path back from the directory or report to the original record. The two cards address gaps in the navigation chain; they are not an endorsement of the cache. If a consumer cannot reach the original record, they should record where the path first breaks and must not substitute another compiled output.

During review, first check whether those three pieces of run evidence can still be found for the current revision, then check separately whether the exit action has an independent rollback state. Only when both are clear can the cache continue to serve as a secondary entry point. If the same input yields a different result for another actual consumer, or if the original run evidence can no longer be rechecked, restore the old entry point and reopen this decision.

DOC-28 contain an on-call record of a failed run; it can serve as a reference from a neighboring run, but does not change the choice made here between cached data and original run evidence.

The ESCB-003 record first documented that the original input had already been rolled back while the expiry action still pointed to the new artifact; later, the original input after rollback was confirmed, and a separate item was opened for the expiry action associated with the new artifact. Both can easily be obscured by "current," but they do not have the same root cause.

# Postmortem on the env Caller's Dual-Version Records

This postmortem preserves an incident involving the misreading of old integration-testing records. The "current revision" in the entry looked unremarkable at the time; only later did it become clear that the same location carried the current states of two revisions at once. The problem was not that readers had failed to see the result, but that the result looked enough like an answer to obscure the old records, the inputs after the rollback, and the actions that still pointed to the new artifacts.

At no point did the page recast "placing the current revision for two revisions in the same entry" as "the two revisions have been confirmed to behave differently." The former describes the display relationship within the entry; the latter requires two sets of invocation samples that can be attributed separately. The available material has not supplied such samples. This distinction repeatedly needed to be set straight during the subsequent review.

The initial clue that prompted a look back was that aggregation serialization did not match the old records. This was not a complete failure chain, nor had any particular revision been proven to have been written incorrectly. The old records show only this: while checking serialization against the existing content, someone saw a deviation that could not be explained immediately; at the same time, the entry could not establish which set of records it was displaying.

The short note from the first version is still preserved below. Its wording is rough, but it is closer to what was observed at the time than the later wording that condensed it to "the current revision is wrong."

> scroll context can be restored, and why the late-static factory changed is still unknown.

The first half of this sentence describes a localized recovery, while the second half is an unknown explicitly recorded at the time. Writing them together does not mean that the factory change caused the recovery, nor that the recovery resolved the serialization deviation. Early readers once linked the three things into a single repair path based on paragraph order; that reading was later abandoned.

## Objects Preserved at the Time of Discovery

The initial response was not to keep running, but to stop further retries and preserve the entry content and old records in `docs/adj-env/incidents/env-client-integration-two-record-versions-not-merged.md`. The retries were not stopped because a fix had already been found, nor because integration testing could never be run again. The reason was simpler: once two sets of current states had been mixed into the entry, producing another new result would only make "current" look more like the only version, without explaining where each of the two previously displayed values had come from.

Preserving the original entry did not amount to acknowledging that it was complete or correct. What it preserved was the relationship between the objects visible at the time of discovery: in the same entry, both revisions appeared with a current status. If it had simply been overwritten with what was displayed later, people looking back would only have seen the page after recovery, and would have had no way to confirm that the anomaly had been a mixing of records rather than a single result becoming invalid.

The first version also preserved four items at different levels:

- the current states of the two revisions in the entry;
- aggregation serialization did not match the old records;
- scroll context can be restored;
- the change in the late-static factory had not yet been explained.

These items should not be collapsed into the single statement "integration debugging failed and then recovered." The entry state describes how the record is presented; the serialization divergence describes a question raised by a comparison; scroll context is a phenomenon along a local call path; factory is an unattributed parallel change. The fact that they appeared in the same context does not automatically make them part of the same causal chain.

The first version also left "Missing timestamp: ____." This blank has still not been filled with the time the record was organized, the card creation time, or the time of the rollback action. What is missing here are the timestamps for when each of the two revisions entered the same entry point, not when someone later read the page. Replacing the early write times with timestamps from subsequent activities would collapse discovery, organization, rollback, and execution into a single moment.

The early impact assessment was also intentionally narrow. What can be confirmed is that people viewing the entry might have treated the old revision as the current integration state; when checking aggregation serialization against the old record, they might have seen results inconsistent with observations near the entry point. No evidence shows that all callers went through this entry point, nor that every request encountered the same problem.

## Recovery Misread Later

scroll context can be restored; it is one of the only direct signs of recovery left in the document. It indicates that at least one piece of context became available again in a later observation. It does not indicate that the entry content has been merged; it does not indicate that the old record has been reconstructed; nor does it indicate that aggregation serialization has returned to the state described by the old record.

The second version revised the ordering of the first version. The early wording first mentioned serialization divergence and then scroll context recovery, making it read as though the latter repaired the former. The misreading caused by that ordering is retained here, but not its conclusion. The evidence provides no common input, common revision, or causal link between the two observations.

"user-path recovery" was also a broad phrase used during the later organization. It is now retained only as legacy wording. It should not be expanded to "all callers recovered," because no scope was defined at the time and no results were broken down by caller. The boundary we can maintain here is: a local recovery occurred; the root cause remains unresolved.

Likewise, the local recovery should not be attributed to a particular rollback, exit action, or index loading. They all appeared in the subsequent record compilation, but each item describes something different. Turning them into a repair relationship based on temporal proximity would once again recreate the misjudgment caused by conflating them at the entry point.

## The Second Version's Relative Timeline

The second round of compilation did not invent specific timestamps; instead, it placed the known relationships in sequence. It is not a runtime log, nor does it mean that every row came from the same request.

| Relative position | What was seen at the time | Handling retained |
|---|---|---|
| Initial discovery | One entry contained the current state of two revisions | Preserve the entry and the old record |
| Same context | aggregation serialization differed from the old record | Do not close it out on the basis of a single cause |
| Subsequently | scroll context could be restored | Mark separately as local recovery |
| Review stage | late-static factory could not be attributed | Leave for investigation |
| Organization stage | The early timestamp was still missing | Do not fill it with a later date |

The value of this table is not in fabricating precise timestamps, but in avoiding conflating different types of "later" into a single operation. Mixed content at the entry, restoration of a particular context, someone revisiting an old record, and rollback or indexing actions appearing in subsequent cards are not the same thing.

The second version also added a reading-path diagram. The diagram shows what to determine first when faced with a mixed entry, not an execution relationship that has already been confirmed.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Caller integration test entry] --> B[Current states of the two revisions]
    B --> C{Record sources distinguishable}
    C -- No --> D[Retain entry content]
    D --> E[Compare with old records]
    C -- Yes --> F[Review integration test results separately]
    E --> G[aggregation serialization]
    E --> H[scroll context]
    E --> I[late-static factory pending investigation]
```

The "review integration test results separately" step in the diagram is the next step once the condition is met, and does not mean that two complete sets of results were later obtained. Older pages sometimes described this kind of judgment step as if verification had already ended; this is now considered outdated wording. What is actually retained here is the decision not to continue overwriting the live state when the sources cannot be distinguished.

## Rollback did not bring all objects back

ESCB-003 Later records make it necessary to explain "rollback" in separate parts. The card first records a state: the original input has been rolled back, but the expiration action still points to the new artifact. Subsequent records confirm the original input after rollback and open a separate expiration action for the new artifact.

This set of materials does not explain how the two revisions initially entered the caller integration test entry. What it can correct is another simplification: "the original input has been rolled back" cannot be treated as meaning that all subsequent actions returned to the old object. Rollback confirms the original input; the expiration action still pointing to the new artifact is a separate processing track.

An older version contained wording roughly like "continue checking the current entry after rollback"; this no longer applies. Not because the entry can no longer be viewed, but because the entry's current state is insufficient to distinguish three objects: the original input before the event, the original input confirmed by the rollback action, and the new artifact still pointed to by the expiration action. Collapsing these three into one "version" would cause the action corresponding to the new artifact to be mistakenly treated as completed.

After ESCB-003, the follow-up entered processing, indicating that someone began handling the separated-out matter. It cannot retroactively fill the missing time field in the first version, nor prove which write caused the aggregation serialization deviation. The fact that work has started is a processing status, not a historical account of the earliest entry contents.

In this postmortem, the impact of the rollback is documented only up to this point. No material lists which callers used the new artifact, and no material states whether the separately opened expiration action later ended. Expanding "opened separately" into a complete migration conclusion would exceed the scope actually documented in this incident record.

## The exit action that was not queued

ESCB-008 leave another gap in the handling path. The card initially left the owner slot for env · Client Integration vacant, while limiting the temporary assignee to handling expiry actions, without assigning long-term meaning to the integration testing work. Later records mention that the expiry action had already passed and that the exit entry point was not queued in that round; work on the item subsequently resumed.

This passage can easily be misread as the cause of entry-point mixing. It is not. The vacant owner slot and the exit entry point not being queued can explain why a closing action was not handled at the expected stage; they cannot explain why the same entry point once displayed the current status of two revisions.

Here, "exit entry point" refers to a processing entry point that should be removed from the current integration testing workflow. It is not an exit for user requests, nor is it an alias for a revision. The old records did not explain this term clearly, and some later readers confused it with rollback. The two handle different things: rollback handles the original input, while the exit action handles the end-of-process path that was not queued.

Resuming work on this card also does not mean that long-term responsibility has been clarified. The available records only show that the item moved from the backlog back into progress. The second version described "someone has taken over" in terms close to "someone is now responsible for the issue", which overstates the case; temporarily handling an expiry action is not the same as establishing long-term ownership.

Therefore, this card's role in the retrospective is to preserve an unresolved handling condition: after entry-point mixing occurred, the surrounding closing actions did not simply disappear. It does not establish the root cause, nor does it provide proof that the fault was fixed.

## Another layer of confusion caused by indexing order

ESCB-013 document not a failure to merge the two versions of the records, but a reversal in the order of the indexing time and env-client-integration. Subsequent material classified this as a failure and noted that the current result had been loaded, with the failure remaining behind the person on duty.

Entry-point mixing concerns the source of the records: why the same location contains the current status of two revisions. The reversed indexing order concerns chronology: why the relative order of the event and env-client-integration cannot be read in the usual way. Both anomalies make "current" appear more reliable than history, but they concern different things and cannot be covered by the same conclusion.

"The current result has been loaded" only indicates that a loaded result existed at the time. It does not supply the missing provenance for the two revisions in the earliest entry point, nor does it make the failure automatically disappear at an earlier point in time. The old page placed this sentence in a paragraph near the recovery discussion, which could easily be understood to mean that the old records no longer needed to be reviewed; its original temporal context is now preserved, and it is no longer treated as a signal that the matter is wrapped up.

The reversed indexing chronology also limits how the impact can be described. It makes the records harder to read later: readers may interpret integration testing and indexing in the wrong relative order. But the material does not state that it changed each caller's actual requests, nor does it state that it is directly related to the deviation in aggregation serialization.

Therefore, ESCB-013 is only a temporally adjacent issue here. It helps explain why looking only at the current results is insufficient to reconstruct the history, but it is not included in the root cause of "the two versions of the records not being merged."

## The unsourced explanation was removed

The direction of ESCB-015 is relatively clear: retain the navigation entry point for the current revision and remove the explanatory text that cannot be traced back to a source. Keeping the entry point does not mean it has become a complete answer; removing the explanation does not mean deleting the earlier incident state. What was removed was a passage that could not explain the revision's source, yet could easily be treated by readers as a basis for determining the order.

This action is relevant to the incident state, because the early confusion came not only from two revisions appearing at the same time, but also from someone trying to use an unsourced explanation to determine which came first. The explanatory text looked like a conclusion, but could not be traced back to old records, a specific integration testing session, or a particular write. Keeping it would make uncertainty look like something already confirmed.

The statement in the old version that "the current revision already has an explanation" is now marked as no longer applicable. The revision is still visible, and the navigation entry point is still retained; the change is that visibility is no longer treated as traceability. If the entry point only shows results without explaining their source, readers may still mistake old records for current facts.

This change did not supply the actual write order of the two revisions. It only removed a claim that should not have taken the place of determining the order. The page still retains the original empty entries, rather than using the removal of the explanation to pretend that the history has been reconstructed.

## Where aggregation serialization fits

aggregation serialization is the earliest technical clue on this page. It differed from the old records, prompting people to go back from the results to the entry point and notice that the current states of two revisions were present in the same place. This order of observation should be preserved: first noticing an inconsistency with the old records, then finding that the entry point could not provide reliable attribution; it was not a case of first proving that the two revisions behaved differently in practice, then noticing the serialization deviation.

The old materials did not retain a complete sample, so this serialization result cannot be definitively assigned to either revision. The later cards did not provide this mapping either. Therefore, neither "a serialization error in the new revision" nor "a serialization error in the old records" is a conclusion this page can draw; both formulations would assume that the sources have already been distinguished.

The assessment that can be retained is narrower: if someone checks aggregation serialization against the old records, they may see results that differ from the content around the integration-testing entry point at the time; the two sets of current states at the entry point also prevent immediate attribution of the difference. This assessment is already enough to explain why the choice at the time was to preserve the incident state rather than continue overwriting it.

The second version grouped the serialization clue and the partial recovery in the same set of notes, with wording that made it sound as though the deviation had disappeared with the recovery. That arrangement is now explicitly marked as outdated. aggregation serialization remains an unattributed deviation, and the recovery of scroll context does not automatically provide a conclusion about it.

When reviewing this record later, it is more important to first confirm which old record is being compared than to first infer behavior from the entry point's current state. This is the reading order that emerged from this incident, not a procedure that every caller integration must use.

## late-static factory remains unexplained

The late-static factory has been pending investigation since the first version. It drew attention because it appeared near the entry-point anomaly in the same incident context, not because there was already evidence linking it to record merging, serialization divergence, or recovery actions. Later versions added no material that could supersede "why it changed is still unknown".

There are two reasons to retain it. First, it is indeed part of the incident record, and deleting it would lead later readers to mistakenly think that this lead did not exist at the time. Second, it has never been reliably attributed, and preserving the unknown is more consistent with the existing record than filling in a seemingly plausible explanation.

The roles it cannot serve should also be made explicit: it cannot be called the reason the two versions of the record were not merged; it cannot be called the fix point for aggregation serialization; it cannot be used to explain why scroll context recovered. For all of these relationships, the revision and call results needed for comparison are missing.

At one point, the second version presented "continue investigating factory" as something very much like a next step, but no corresponding results were added later. This incomplete state is now retained rather than edited into a completed investigation. It remains the most direct outstanding technical item on this page.

## Still usable, but outdated assessments

The following statements all appeared in the old records, and they are retained to show where misinterpretations began, not for continued use.

> Old assessment: The revision currently shown at the entry point can serve as the sole baseline for integration testing.

Deprecated. The anomaly is precisely that two revision values are currently visible at the same entry point at the same time. When the source is unclear, the entry point can serve as a place to revisit for review, but cannot serve as the sole baseline.

> Old assessment: Once scroll context has recovered, the divergence in aggregation serialization should have disappeared.

Later overturned. The material confirms only partial recovery of the former, and does not establish any causal relationship or synchronization between it and the latter.

> Old assessment: The change to the late-static factory explains why the two versions of the record were not merged.

Unconfirmed. It remains a change on the periphery of the incident that awaits investigation, not an attribution of the failure's cause.

> Old assessment: After the original input is rolled back, the associated expiration actions will naturally return to their old state.

No longer applicable. ESCB-003 retained the original input after rollback, as well as the expiration actions that still pointed to the new artifact; the latter were split out for separate handling.

These old assessments were not simply deleted, because deleting them would leave only the later, more cautious conclusions and obscure why anyone at the time would have interpreted partial recovery, the current entry point, and the rollback results as the same completed state.

## Impact window and unfinished items

The most direct impact of this anomaly was not a confirmed failure across all callers, but a compressed view of the historical record caused by the current display. Readers of the entry point may treat the old revision as the basis for current integration testing; those comparing serialization may mistake unattributed deviations for the behavior of a particular version; those handling things after the rollback may overlook expiry actions that still point to the new artifact; people reviewing in index order may also encounter env-client-integration and the indexing time in reverse chronological order.

These impacts are not the same. Mixing records at the entry point is a record provenance issue; serialization deviations are clues for comparing behavior; rollback concerns the separation between the original input and subsequent actions; the fact that the exit entry point did not enter the queue represents a gap in the processing path; index inversion is a chronological ordering issue; an unsourced explanation is a pseudo-explanation for the reader. They share the backdrop that "the current state can easily obscure the history", but they cannot be written up as a single root cause.

The questions still remaining on the page are as follows:

- when each of the two revisions entered the same entry point;
- whether the differences in aggregation serialization can be tied to one of those revisions;
- whether the recovery of the scroll context and the other observations merely occurred during the same period;
- whether the changes to the late-static factory were unrelated to the mixing at the entry point;
- whether the early timestamps left blank can be filled in from the original integration-testing materials;
- which callers had made judgments based on the old entry point;
- whether the exit entry point was actually completed after processing resumed on ESCB-008;
- how the expiry action associated with the new artifact eventually ended.

This page is still retained because it documents how the old entry point lost its explanatory value during an anomaly. It is not the current integration guide, nor does it set out new long-term rules for subsequent callers. To revisit the original incident context, the entry point is still at `docs/adj-env/incidents/env-client-integration-two-record-versions-not-merged.md`; to understand the subsequent handling in adjacent areas, refer separately to ESCB-003, ESCB-008, ESCB-013 and ESCB-015.

It does not determine migration status from directory structure: the directory is only a locator clue; what actually needs to be confirmed is whether a given caller has switched to the replacement location and whether the failure context can still be reviewed.

Different entry points can have different schedules, maintainers, and exit criteria, so a record is not automatically linked to another just because the descriptions are similar.
```text
Old entry point ──────> Keep existing callers
  │
  ├── Migrate one caller to the replacement location
  │       │
  │       ├── Retain runtime signals, failure context, and recovery observation window
  │       └── Restore the old entry point when rollback is needed
  │
  └── Unconfirmed callers: keep listing them on the old-entry side
```

The latter two do not need to be turned into an incident report; they only make it possible to revisit the same observation after rollback. If any one of the three is missing, keep the old relationship in place. The replacement location may exist, but do not record the migration as complete.

For each index entry, list the old entry point first, then the replacement location, and finally the known callers. Record a replacement location as migrated only after it has actually been invoked. Do not mark callers that have not yet been checked as complete, and do not remove them from the old-entry list. When a note consists only of a name, with no failure context or caller, retain "Unable to trace back"; do not fill in a migration history by guessing.

Migrate only one known caller at a time. During the trial migration, the old entry point remains readable, and the replacement location serves only this caller. If an anomaly occurs, the recovery action involves only that caller and does not bring back other relationships that have not yet been confirmed. After the observation window ends, decide whether to move to the next batch; without an observation window, stop at this batch.

Rollback does not delete the replacement location. First switch that caller back to the old entry point, then inspect the metric signals using the original failure context and recovery observation window. If the failure context is still present after restoration, record only "Old entry point restored, failure context pending review" in the index. At that point, the restoration action alone cannot be used to attribute the issue to either the old entry point or the replacement location.

Older material once treated "new location visible" as a sign that the migration was close to complete. That judgment remains in the old record, but no longer applies: a new location only shows that it can be located; it does not show that the old entry point has no callers left.
