# Makefile Current Entry Point Migration Index

Old entry points were not removed as soon as replacement locations appeared. This was initially only a brief note, but later became the reason the index continued to be referenced: a relationship in the runtime observability console may already have a new location while still being connected to callers that have not migrated. Old entry points, replacement locations, and callers are therefore kept separately; a tidy directory is no substitute for verifying the actual context.

The earliest draft left only two questions: whether rollback restores only the old entry point, and which callers are still using the old relationship. That draft had no answers, nor did it turn the gaps into conclusions. The material added later mainly covers migration batches and rollback observations; the early unconfirmed items remain unchanged in the index.

## What the index retains

This page covers only the runtime signals, failure contexts, and recovery observation windows associated with metric in Makefile · Operations Observability Board. Each piece of work has its own schedule, maintainer, and exit criteria, so entry points from neighboring projects are not included. Identical entry point names or similar descriptions are not sufficient grounds for merging two records.

The index answers a very narrow question: whether a particular old entry point still has known callers; if a replacement location exists, whether rollback can return to the old relationship. It is not responsible for explaining all runtime signals or determining causes from failure contexts. If a note does not record a caller or context, the index retains the item and marks it as unable to be traced back; do not use text compiled later to fill the gap as though it were a known fact.

| Index column | What is retained | When the status changes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Old entry point | Relationships that are still reachable, known callers, legacy notes | Once each caller has been confirmed to no longer pass through that relationship |
| Replacement location | The current location receiving the migration, callers that have started using it | Indicates availability, not that the old entry point can be deleted |
| Observation location | metric signals, failure contexts, recovery observation windows | For review after migration or rollback |
| Items that cannot be traced back | Entries with only old text or names remaining | Retain until a caller or context is found |

"Current" has always been a relative term within this index, not a permanent entry point name. When an entry point changes again, add a new row linking the old relationship at that time to the new location, rather than rewriting an earlier row. Otherwise, readers may mistakenly believe that the old callers never existed, and will not be able to tell which relationship a particular rollback actually returned to.

The old entry point column is not a list of entry points "about to be taken offline". It first serves two purposes: keeping the original destination available to callers that have not yet migrated, and providing a recoverable path for callers that have tried migrating if an anomaly occurs. The replacement location column is not a "master list of new entry points" either; it records only replacement locations that have already received callers within this index.

## How to record a migration batch

Select one identifiable caller on the old entry point side. Before moving it, record the metric signals currently being observed, the failure contexts that have occurred, and the window to be observed after recovery. Migration can be postponed if the information is incomplete; having the replacement location ready is no substitute for this record.

```text
Old entry point
  │
  ├─ Known caller ──> Replacement location ──> Recovery observation window
  │                                  │
  │                                  ├─ Context can still be reviewed: retain this migration
  │                                  └─ Rollback needed: return to the old entry point
  │
  └─ Unknown caller ──> Keep in the old entry point column
```

Handle only one caller at a time. This keeps changes at the replacement location, the failure context, and the recovery observation window tied to the same migration, rather than mixing them into a batch of relationships being adjusted simultaneously. The old entry point remains in place at this stage; it is not a failure marker, but an available relationship needed for rollback. Having one caller already running at the replacement location does not mean other callersFang Ke can migrate automatically.

After a caller has migrated, the index should record at least one of three statuses: retained at the replacement location, rolled back to the old entry point, or still pending verification because the information is incomplete. Do not lump these three statuses together as "in progress". In particular, a caller that has been rolled back must not be put back on the unmigrated list: it did pass through a replacement location once, but that migration was not retained.

During observation, retain the signals and context descriptions originally seen. Signals becoming stable later must not overwrite the initial failure context; the absence of further anomalies after rollback also does not allow you to infer that the replacement location played no part in that context. The index only needs to tell later readers where observation began, which window it ended in, and whether this migration was retained or rolled back.

The starting point for the next batch is not that "several new locations already exist", but whether the observations left by the previous batch are sufficient to distinguish the old relationship from the replacement location. If the recovery observation window has not ended, or a known caller still cannot be confirmed, stay with the original batch. This keeps old entry points around longer, but does not prematurely mark a set of contexts that have not yet been disentangled as complete.

## Records after rollback

The old approach was straightforward: when the context after migration can no longer be observed, first return that caller to the old entry point, then observe the metric signals using the same recovery observation window. That sequence remains here, but it is not a rule for attributing all anomalies. If the context persists after recovery, the index should state only that the migration has been rolled back and the context still needs investigation, rather than casually assigning responsibility to either entry point.

The original draft left `release rollback` as an unconfirmed question about callers. The rollback observations added later did not turn it into a general rule; they only confirmed that rollback should restore the old relationship, rather than continue advancing an unconfirmed replacement location. After the old entry point is restored, unmigrated callers remain in the old entry point column; callers that have attempted migration are recorded separately as rolled back, so that both groups are not read as "unmigrated".

Completing rollback also does not mean the replacement location can be cleared out. The replacement location should remain in that row, so readers can see where the caller moved out of and where it returned to. Only deleting the replacement location would deprive later failure contexts of a before-and-after comparison of the migration. The index does not need to invent a cause for this, only to preserve the relationship and observation location.

Before retiring an old entry point, check three things individually: whether known callers no longer pass through the old relationship; whether the replacement location can still be located from the index; and whether the failure context and recovery observation window still have records available for review. The third check does not require reinterpreting the incident, but prevents the observation location from being lost along with the old entry point when it is removed.

If any of these cannot be confirmed, the old entry point remains in the index. This retention does not mean all old notes must be maintained indefinitely. Some notes have only a name remaining and can no longer be associated with a specific caller or context; this text retains its "cannot be traced back" status so that people encountering old links can recognize it, and is no longer treated as a basis for new migrations.

## Earlier judgments kept on record

Early versions placed "the new location has already appeared in the directory" alongside the pre-migration checks. This wording could easily be read as a completion criterion and no longer applies. Directory visibility can still help locate the replacement location, but completion depends only on whether the actual callers have migrated and whether the old entry point still retains the relationship. The old sentence was not deleted so that it can explain why some old entry points still exist after directory changes.

Another old note described the replacement location and the old relationship as mutually exclusive states: as though, once the new location became available, only historical text remained on the old side. The actual migration batches did not support this wording. The index now allows both sides to coexist: one side has callers that have not yet migrated, while the other has callers that have undergone trial migrations or have been retained at the replacement location. The old note remains archived and is not used to assess the next batch.

Explanatory text that cannot be traced back should not be reworked either. It can only help identify that an old name once appeared, not establish its callers, failure context, or exit criteria. Retaining a navigation entry point and retaining explanatory text are two different things.

## Entry points for later cleanup

ESCD-004 documented a comparison between exit actions and rollback of the old relationship, after which handling began. The related actions were to replay the rollback and check whether the old edge had actually disappeared. This can help locate subsequent work, but cannot replace the item-by-item assessments in the index: whether the old edge has disappeared must be considered together with caller status and the recovery observation window.

ESCD-010 took a different direction: retain the navigation entry point for the current revision and remove explanatory text that cannot be traced back. This action did not supply the missing failure context or turn the original gaps into completed migrations. The scope of responsibility for subsequent work was later adjusted because the issue lay in another part of the implementation; this likewise does not imply that a particular entry point has been fully handled.

This page therefore still retains only entry point relationships, caller statuses, and the locations of signals and contexts. Navigation for the current revision can still be used; do not rewrite removed explanations from memory. Entries in the old index whose sources still cannot be identified can simply remain marked as outdated.

## Reading order

Find the corresponding entry from `docs/adj-makefile/migration/current-entry-legacy-entry-migration-index.md`, read the old entry point column first, then the replacement location and known callers. If the entry includes a failure context or recovery observation window, return to the same location for review after migration or rollback; if only an old name remains, first treat it as an item pending verification, and do not add it to the next batch.

For known callers, record migration, retention, and rollback as separate statuses. For unknown callers, simply keep them on the old entry point side. A caller absent from the index does not automatically belong to the replacement location; add a separate row when it is discovered. This lets readers distinguish relationships that can be rolled back from historical text, even if old paths remain incompletely cleaned up for a long time.

This page preserves a period when an old entry point may still be useful. Current navigation remains available, and explanations that cannot be traced back are no longer used as a basis; the remaining entries without context continue in their original outdated state.

# makefile-operations Maintainer Map

`makefile-operations-observability` has two kinds of work that are easy to conflate: entry points, exit actions, and temporary coverage for the live context; and long-term technical judgment. The former can be handled by Makefile · Operations Observability Board, while the latter still needs to follow the relevant maintainer relationships. This page does not combine the two kinds of issue into a single answer.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Actual user] --> B[Current entry point or live context]
    B --> C{Which part does the issue concern?}
    C -->|Broken links, timing, due actions| D[Operations Monitoring Console staff on duty]
    C -->|Long-term technical interpretation| E[Long-term maintainer or vacancy]
    D --> F[Temporary assignee or source/adopter]
    E --> G[Provide a conclusion for this part]
```

The entry file is still `docs/adj-makefile/ownership/makefile-operations-observability-current-maintainer-map.md`. When entering from the current revision, first have the actual user record the first broken link they encounter; until the entry point is restored, do not substitute a similarly named page for it. ESCD-002 remain here as a navigation card for this kind of broken link.

| Item in the live context | First contact | What to do on receipt | Does not answer for |
|---|---|---|---|
| Navigation path in the current revision | Makefile · Operations Observability Board staff on duty | Record the first broken link the actual user sees and preserve the path they took to get there. | The source page's long-term maintainer. |
| This page's file and the temporary entry point to the live context | Makefile · Operations Observability Board staff on duty | Determine whether this is an entry-point failure, an exit action, or a takeover action, then route it accordingly. | The maintainer responsible for long-term technical interpretation. |
| Exit action | Temporary assignee | Handle actions that are already due and need to be handed off; retain the handoff time with the live context. | The long-term owner who remains unconfirmed after the takeover. |
| End of temporary coverage | Long-term maintainer: vacant | If no one has signed to accept the handoff, leave the slot vacant and report the unaccepted status back at the entry point. | The most recent person to reply to the issue. |
| Two records both named "current entry point" | Each record's source and adopter | Record the source and adopter for each one, then check whether they actually point to the same object. | The maintainer of the other record with the same name. |
| Events, `makefile-operations-observability`, and index timestamps | Makefile · Operations Observability Board staff on duty | Line up the timestamps from all three places; record any unexplained time difference separately. | A technical owner inferred from chronological order. |

Temporary coverage is not shorthand for long-term ownership. During testing, someone who could modify the fixtures was needed to take over. That shows that an actionable handoff point was needed at the time, not that the person gained long-term authority over technical interpretation. The handoff record left afterward already includes a handoff time, but the acceptance signature at the exit entry point is still blank; this is why the table above separates "exit action" from "long-term maintainer." ESCD-003 can be used to revisit this vacancy, but should not be used as grounds to fill in a name.

Entry points with the same name must not be merged based on name alone, either. ESCD-009 concern separating the sources: one record first states where it came from, while the other states who actually adopted it. Until both pieces are in place, the Operations Monitoring Console only retains each one's live context and does not confirm a shared maintainer relationship on behalf of both sides.

Timing issues follow a different path. ESCD-008 note that the chronological order of the index timestamp and `makefile-operations-observability` needs to be checked. When this kind of discrepancy occurs, the person on duty is responsible for retaining the event, object, and index timestamp side by side; if the time difference cannot be explained, keep it as a separate issue rather than folding it into the exit handoff.

Include only the minimum context when handing off: the revision entered, the first visible broken link or time difference, whether any actions are due, and whether an acceptance signature is already present. When a long-term technical question comes in and the maintainer has not yet been confirmed, record only the vacancy and the handoff destination at the entry point; project coordination can arrange a window, but does not make technical conclusions on the maintainer's behalf.

Maintaining this page means updating the map, not overwriting the previous live context. When adding someone to take over, also state whether they are taking over an exit action or the live context; the corresponding vacancy can be closed only when a long-term owner is added. # Horizon Compatibility Freeze Decision Record

The Horizon compatibility freeze was later often reduced to "keep legacy calls". That was not the original intent. The review addressed whether the transport-config entry point should be reinterpreted during the freeze, and whether the downstream adoption window could serve as a basis for changing the entry point. Keeping the entry point for now, leaving the window out of this round of changes, and no longer silently emulating unsupported legacy behavior were three decisions made in the same comparison; remembering only one makes this decision seem broader than it originally was.

The materials at the time came from Northline Systems' compatibility review. Only two options were on the table. One would retain the current entry point, leaving already observable calls on the existing path; the other would first adjust the adoption window, then use that window to handle the transition between new and legacy calls. The latter wording can make the window sound like a mere scheduling tool, but once it is used to determine how a call should be interpreted, it already affects entry point semantics, not just handoff timing.

The initial draft presented the first option as the safer choice. That judgment rested on a premise that now seems too broad: the fact that existing calls could continue to pass through the entry point seemed sufficient to justify retaining it. This premise failed to distinguish two things. The available materials could only establish that observed inputs and results were worth using as comparison points; they could not establish that calls with similar names, calls used historically, or calls not yet observed should automatically receive the same treatment. The old paragraph remains here to explain why the boundaries were not made clear during the freeze, not to elevate it into a long-term position.

## The Two Options Compared at the Time

The benefit of retaining the current transport-config entry point was not that it proved suitable for every call forever, but that the freeze would not need to reclassify calls based on migration assumptions. The existing entry point would continue to handle public calls already routed to it, and inputs and serialized results could still be compared in one place during follow-up review. The cost was direct: once legacy behavior was explicitly outside the scope of support, adopters could not expect the transport layer to add another layer of seemingly successful compatibility results based on the old shape.

The appeal of adjusting the adoption window was also concrete. It could make the downstream adoption transition clearer and avoid squeezing every change into a single entry point change. But this option lacked a necessary prerequisite: the review did not know what each category of downstream calls actually supplied to the entry point, nor what serialized output those calls ultimately produced. Without paired records, the window would change from "migration timing" into a rule for "guessing caller intent based on impressions". Even apparent success would then provide no way to tell whether the call itself had been adapted or the entry point had swallowed differences that should have surfaced.

Therefore, the decision in this round was to retain the entry point, not to approve the window. Deferring the window was not a declaration that it had no value either; it simply was not allowed to fill gaps in the evidence. One view raised during the review was that providing a broader window first could keep transition-period problems under control. The objection was that, if a broad window rested on unchecked calls, the results obtained later could no longer be interpreted: it would be unclear whether the call was inherently compatible or the window had made an undeclared choice on its behalf. The freeze was not the right stage to leave behind behavior that could not be distinguished in this way.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Retain the current transport-config entry point"] --> C["Scope approved in this round"]
    B["Adjust the downstream adoption window"] --> D["Deferred"]
    E["Covered by existing evidence"] --> C
    E --> D
```

"Covered by existing evidence" in the diagram was not a complete inventory of calls. At the time, it meant only that the review was willing to decide on the scope that could already be checked, without treating the missing parts as compatible by default. Some later paraphrased this as "retain it if there are legacy calls", which is too crude. Whether a legacy call had occurred and whether that call had sufficient input and output records for comparison are not the same question.

## Handling Legacy Behavior

The requirement left in the meeting materials was:

> keep unsupported legacy behavior visibly retired instead of silently emulating it

The point here was not to make all legacy calls disappear immediately, but to avoid hiding unsupported behavior behind a layer of emulation. If the entry point silently filled in the old shape for legacy behavior, callers might see only a result with no error, without knowing whether they were relying on a still-supported path or a historical accident that had been preserved. The review preferred to let migration differences surface and did not agree to use silent emulation to smooth things over in the short term.

This decision did leave some inconvenience to downstream adopters. Retaining the entry point did not mean providing a safety net for old shapes; visibly retiring legacy behavior did not mean that migration arrangements were complete either. The gap between the two was not filled with transport-config at the time. The reason was not that the downstream window was considered unimportant, but that there were no materials to distinguish which adopters already had alternative paths and which had simply not yet been observed. Mixing these two cases into the same layer of compatibility handling would only delay the appearance of problems.

Another approach raised was to make exceptions only for legacy inputs that "looked safe". This approach was not included in the decision. At the time, the supposed safety relied mainly on recollections of call sites rather than paired behavior records; the entry point should not carry such memory-based judgments. Even if a call had appeared stable in the past, that did not establish that it was suitable for continued interpretation by the window or emulation logic.

## Evidence Retention Requirements Added After Follow-up Review

The initial draft said only "retain the output", which was too broad and could easily mix screenshots, excerpts, and migration expectations together. During follow-up review, it was expanded into the following requirement:

> Start from a reproducible public call, retain the exact input and raw serialized output, and separate observed behavior from migration assumptions.

This requirement split the discussion into two levels. The first was to start from a reproducible public call and retain the exact input that the call actually supplied to the entry point, along with the raw serialized output produced when the request was serialized. Only when those two were matched could there be a discussion of whether an adjustment had changed the call's meaning. Seeing a piece of output alone, or knowing only that an adopter wanted to maintain its pace within the window, was not enough to judge the entry point's behavior.

The second level was to separate observed behavior from migration assumptions. The former could describe the serialized result produced when an input passed through the current entry point; the latter could express how an adopter hoped to arrange the transition. Observed results could not automatically become migration commitments, and migration assumptions could not, in reverse, prove that a behavior was already supported. This was the main reason the window was deferred: at the time, it could not be shown that the window affected only adoption timing without taking part in interpreting calls.

Tracing back through `lib/Elastica/Client.php` and the related call names was intended to recover the location of the entry point involved in this comparison, not to establish permanent ownership of that file. The file's location could help verify the relationship between a public call and transport-config, but it could not replace paired input and output records. Reducing the decision to whether a particular file would change would also miss the interpretation risks originally introduced by the adoption window.

## Misreadings Left by the Initial Draft

The initial draft's closing wording was "Do not split the transport-config entry point for now. The window can remain under discussion, but migration assumptions should not be written into the entry point rules until records of reproducible calls are available." It still describes the working state at the time, but was later read as "the entry point will be split as soon as the records arrive". That was not the conclusion after follow-up review. The purpose of the records was to make the window comparable again, not to endorse either option in advance.

The initial draft also listed "existing calls can pass through" as a reason to favor retaining the entry point. That statement no longer applies. Passing through could only show that the particular observed inputs and outputs at the time did not provide a basis for splitting the entry point; it could not extend compatibility coverage to unobserved calls. This correction is retained because old links still lead people to the abbreviated judgment in the initial draft; simply deleting the old wording would instead leave later readers unable to understand why the window had been mistaken for a predetermined next step.

DOC-44 record handoff pointers for the downstream adoption window. The materials adopters need to take with them during the switch can be retained there; the handoff process is not rewritten here as entry point rules. The decision on this page still has only two points: maintain the current transport-config entry point within the scope of existing evidence; keep unsupported legacy behavior explicitly retired rather than silently emulating it.

The unresolved parts should also remain as they were: whether the existing materials covered all public calls that would be affected by the window was not confirmed at the time; if different adopters assigned different migration meanings to the same input, those differences could not simply be pushed into the entry point; exactly how "visibly retired" would be presented in adopters' materials was also not decided in this review. These gaps explain why the record is still cited, while also limiting the extent to which it can be cited.

# transport-config Offline Regression Entry-Point Guide

This review still starts at `lib/Elastica/Transport/Http.php`. Not because its name looks most like the answer, but because the set of search terms in transport-config first narrowed the reading scope to the transport side. After opening the file, the person taking over should treat it as the gateway into the repository: confirm whether the config-related path passes through here, then decide which call site to follow next. The file itself is not the conclusion about the offline regression evidence, nor is it meant to explain the entire Elastica PHP Client request flow.

This review keeps a very short reading path:

```text
transport-config
      |
      v
lib/Elastica/Transport/Http.php
      |
one direct caller
      |
first consumer of offline regression evidence
```

The 'one direct caller' in the diagram is deliberately the level of detail to retain. During the review, first use `Http.php` to find one direct link that connects, and confirm that the match is not merely something that also has transport or config in its name. Only after this hop is established should you check whether the next location actually reads, passes along, or depends on offline regression evidence. There is no need to first collect every file that references the transport layer; that would mix entry-point search with call relationships and make it difficult to tell where the evidence is first actually used.

At the start, keep brief notes for three locations: file, call, and consumer. For the file location, write `lib/Elastica/Transport/Http.php`; for the call location, record only the direct adjacency already observed and do not guess a missing symbol name; for the consumer location, use the first place where offline regression evidence appears in actual use. None of the three is a directory. They are there so the next reader can resume from the most recently confirmed location after an interruption, without having to re-filter all transport-config hits from scratch.

offline regression transcript serves only as locator material along this path. First use its entry name and result context to verify that the path being read is still from the same context; then check whether the evidence mentioned in the transcript connects to the current call edge. The files, terms, and results listed in the transcript do not by themselves constitute a call graph. If an item only shares a name and has no link from the preceding node, it remains a signpost. Leaving it to the side is more useful than forcing it onto the main path, because a later review will show that it was checked without mistaking it for a consumer.

When many files share a name, it is easy to conflate 'worth opening' with 'already reached'. The former is determined solely by the search terms: it means the file may be related to transport-config. The latter must be supported by a direct reference or call: it means the review has reached the next node from the current one. In practice, start from `Http.php` and find one direct call. If that location cannot carry the path forward toward the evidence, demote it to a signpost; do not extend the path downward based on the name. Only the relation that connects the previous and next locations belongs in the main-line record.

This also defines what 'first consumer' means. It is not the first file where offline regression evidence appears as a text hit, nor the earliest name in the transcript; it is the first location encountered while following the confirmed call direction where that evidence has an actual use. If, before that point, you have seen only comments, similar names, or standalone offline-regression material, it still must not be recorded as a consumer. This distinction lets the review stop early without losing the direction needed for continued reading.

The review did not turn missing details into definite facts. The material currently available does not establish a stable function name, line number, test name, or command output that can be reproduced verbatim, so the record stays at three levels: file path, one direct caller, and first consumer. This is not hiding the gap: when someone reaches the call site, the concrete symbol can be added at the second node; once the evidence's ownership or generation method is known, it can be added at the third node. Until those are confirmed, a filename cannot stand in for a function name, and the name of the offline regression context cannot stand in for a call edge.

There is one explicit stopping point: after the first consumer, if the evidence's ownership, generation method, or next call relationship requires explanation from another owner, do not infer it from materials in adjacent projects. This records the entry path from transport-config to the first real consumer; it does not extend into deeper transport, test, or release details. When stopping at this level, retain the most recently confirmed call location and the corresponding transcript context; anyone continuing can use them to open the original location.

DOC-46 can serve as another local navigation path, but should not be mixed into this one. It records a deviation in a public API review rotation, which is a different issue from the file entry, call adjacency, and offline regression evidence consumption point documented here. Only if the review finds that the entry-point deviation and that review need to be handled in parallel should you switch to DOC-46; do not use that record to fill in the call relationship missing from this page.

Only two conclusions are stable enough to reuse at this point: `Http.php` is the anchor file for the transport-config review; after leaving it, the goal is to confirm one direct caller, then find the first real consumer of offline regression evidence. All other same-named files remain signposts. The deeper link remains at the call site that still needs confirmation, and any follow-up notes should start there.

title: Public API Review Discrepancy Postmortem

versions.body:
# Public API Review Discrepancy Postmortem

The public API review rotation originally had a clearly defined verification window. The result actually visible during the window did not match the original arrangement: the request shape had already exposed a discrepancy, but the behavior the arrangement expected to preserve did not receive the same confirmation. The team therefore did not continue treating it as a pass/fail for a single interface; instead, this round was first treated as a discrepancy in the handoff.

The main impact was on the window itself. The planned review could not be completed in the original sequence, and subsequent judgments could only rely on the NullTransport request capture from that time. The capture can show what request was sent at the time, but it cannot replace a complete assessment of public API behavior; in particular, it cannot on its own attribute the issue to a specific part of Client.php, or to a downstream caller.

The timeline is brief:

- When it was first discovered, the visible result did not match the rotation plan, and the discrepancy was not immediately attributed to a cause.
- The NullTransport request capture was then retained to avoid having only a verbal impression left after the window ended.
- After the temporary recovery was completed, the review arrangement could continue, but the recovery did not mean that the cause had been found.
- What remains unconfirmed is whether the discrepancy came from the review arrangement, request construction, or continued emulation of legacy behavior at the boundary.

The control point added this time was `keep unsupported legacy behavior visibly retired instead of silently emulating it`. Its meaning at the time was narrow: unsupported legacy behavior should be visible to reviewers, rather than being masked by silent compatibility that hides the gap between the request and the expectation. It was not a root-cause conclusion, nor did it turn behavior that had not yet been reviewed in the window into a confirmed compatibility commitment.

This record is retained as an account of the observations at the time. If revisited later, the review can only restart from that capture and the review arrangement at the time; there is not enough material here to resolve the open point to a definite cause.

# Troubleshooting Tree for Maintenance Ownership Results

The ticket says refresh is complete, but the result still can't be verified.

```text
Results differ
├─ The call entry point for query-dsl is unclear
│  └─ Stop with the party that requested refresh; don't assign people based on the ticket's status
└─ Call entry point can be identified
   ├─ Record the version used
   └─ Compare the offline regression transcript with the same input
      ├─ Outputs differ: retain both records and investigate version differences
      └─ Outputs match: then check the downstream adoption window
```

If either the entry point or version is missing, don't keep rerunning it as a vote.
